---
title: "Day 5 — Capstone: choosing a track"
---

## Overview

Day 5 is one module, chosen from three. Each track is a full seven-hour build that ends
in a short written report. All three use the machinery you built on Days 1 to 4; none
introduces a new framework, and each one builds its new ideas up from first principles
on the page, so you do not need to have met flows, diffusion models or causal models
before.

| Track | What you build | Builds on | Choose if |
|---|---|---|---|
| [A — Normalising flows](m15a-flows.qmd) | RealNVP affine-coupling flow in JAX, used as a variational family against the hierarchical-uplift funnel; compared with mean-field VI and HMC | Modules 8, 10, 11 | You want to go deeper into variational inference and expressive approximating families |
| [B — Score-based diffusion](m15b-diffusion.qmd) | VP-SDE forward process, denoising score matching, Euler–Maruyama reverse sampler, probability-flow ODE with Hutchinson log-likelihood, on backbone torsion-angle data | Modules 1, 7, 8 | You want generative modelling as continuous-time latent-variable inference |
| [C — Structural causal models](m15c-scm.qmd) | A `do` handler on your effect-handler PPL, abduction–action–prediction counterfactuals by posterior inference over exogenous noise, twin networks, on an ad-spend SCM | Modules 12, 13 | You want to connect inference to intervention and counterfactual questions |

Each track page follows the usual template. The report is specified in the
[report template](report-template.qmd), which is the same for all tracks with
track-specific prompts.

## What each track is, in plain terms

**Track A — Normalising flows.** On Day 2 you approximated a posterior with
independent Gaussians, and on Day 3 you saw that this gets variances wrong. For a
hierarchical model it is worse: the posterior is funnel-shaped and the independent
Gaussians miss most of the uncertainty about how different the groups are. A
normalising flow fixes this by starting from a simple distribution and passing it
through a learned, invertible warp. Because the warp is invertible, you can compute the
density of the result exactly, so all of Day 2's machinery still applies, with a far
more flexible shape. You build the warp from scratch, fit it to the funnel, and
measure how much closer it gets to the HMC answer than the Day 2 fit did.

**Track B — Score-based diffusion.** This track turns inference around: instead of
inferring unknowns from data, you learn a model that generates data like yours and can
tell you how probable any point is. The method is to take a data point, add a small
amount of noise, add a little more, and continue until it is pure noise; then train a
network to undo one small step at a time. Starting from noise and running the trained
network backwards produces new data. The track shows that this is a latent-variable
model with a fixed variational posterior, that the training objective is a kind of
ELBO, and that a related deterministic process gives exact likelihoods. The data are
two-dimensional protein backbone angles with three clusters.

**Track C — Structural causal models.** Everything before Day 5 answered "given what
I observed, what is plausible?". Decisions often need "what happens if I *do* this?" and
"what would have happened last week if I had done that instead?". Those are not
conditional probabilities, and a model of the data's joint distribution cannot answer
them. A structural causal model adds one ingredient, a direction of cause for each
variable, and with it both questions become computable. The surprising part, and the
reason this track belongs in this workshop, is that the "what would have happened"
question is a Bayesian inference problem over the model's noise terms, which the PPL
and engines from Days 2 to 4 solve as they are. The example is a marketing model of
seasonality, ad spend, traffic and conversions.

## How to choose

- **Choose A** if you enjoyed Days 2 and 3 most and want to see how the gap between
  variational inference and sampling is closed in practice. It is the most
  self-contained track and the best choice if you are behind on Day 4. Expect to think
  about Jacobians, invertibility and optimisation stability.
- **Choose B** if you want to understand the generative models behind current image,
  audio and protein-design systems from the ground up rather than from a library. It
  has the most new mathematics (a stochastic differential equation and an ordinary
  one) but each piece is derived on the page, and the code is the shortest of the
  three. Expect to think about noise, time and numerical integration.
- **Choose C** if your work involves decisions, experiments, attribution or
  "what if" questions, and you want to see how a probabilistic program answers them.
  It has the least new mathematics and the most new concepts; the difficulty is in
  keeping three kinds of question distinct. Expect to think about graphs, mechanisms
  and what a model can and cannot know from logs.

If you are unsure, read the "problem in plain terms" section of each track page; they
are written to be read in ten minutes each.

## Time budget

| Block | Time |
|---|---|
| Background and derivations | 2 h |
| Steps 1 to 4 (core build with tests) | 3 h |
| Step 5 (experiment for the report) | 1 h |
| Report | 1 h |

## Prerequisites

Track A requires passing checkpoints for Modules 8 and 11. Track B requires Modules 7
and 8. Both also build their networks from the MLP of
[Module 14](../day4/m14-vae.qmd), Step 1 (`pytest tests/m14 -k step1`, about fifteen
minutes on its own). Track C requires Modules 12 and 13. Participants who are behind on
Day 4 should do Module 14 Step 1 and then choose Track A or B.

## Working in pairs

Tracks may be done in pairs. If so, both participants submit the same code and separate
reports, and the report must say which experiment each person ran.
